title: Oil Hits $97 as Iran Fires Missiles at Kuwait and Bahrain. The Deal Everyone Was Waiting For Is Nowhere Close.
excerpt: Fresh hostilities erupt overnight as Iranian missiles target Gulf states. Brent jumps past $97. Diplomacy has stalled. And the world's largest commodity trader says the market is still underpricing the risk.
body:
The deal was supposed to be days away. On Monday, President Trump said negotiations with Iran were "continuing" and a ceasefire extension would come within a week. On Wednesday morning, Iranian missiles were flying at Kuwait and Bahrain.

Brent crude jumped more than 1% to $97.05 a barrel in early Asian trade. West Texas Intermediate rose to $94.77. Both benchmarks hit one-week highs. The Strait of Hormuz — which carried a fifth of the world's oil before the war began on February 28 — remains largely shut.

What Happened Overnight

Iran's Revolutionary Guards Corps launched ballistic missiles at the US Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain and at targets in Kuwait, according to Iranian state media. The IRGC said the strikes were in response to a US attack on a communications tower on Qeshm Island, near the Strait of Hormuz.

US Central Command said all the attacks either failed or were intercepted. Two missiles aimed at Kuwait fell short or broke apart in flight. Three missiles targeting Bahrain were shot down. The US military also downed Iranian drones targeting civilian ships and struck back at Qeshm Island.

Separately, the IRGC said it had attacked a vessel it identified as "Panaya" with missiles, calling it retaliation for a US strike on an Iranian tanker near Hormuz. Iran warned that "disrupting the security of the Strait of Hormuz will carry a heavy price for the US military."

Why the Deal Isn't Happening

The gap between American and Iranian positions remains enormous. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, testifying before Congress on Tuesday, declared bluntly: "The war is over." Democratic Senator Cory Booker disagreed — sharply. Rubio then clarified that the US would only offer sanctions relief if Iran gives up its nuclear program entirely.

Iran wants the opposite: access to billions in frozen oil revenues, waivers on crude exports, the lifting of a US blockade on its ports, and continued leverage over the strait. Iranian media reported that Tehran has not communicated with Washington for several days, though Trump insisted talks were ongoing.

The pattern has become grimly familiar. Every week brings a new round of optimistic statements followed by military escalation. The ceasefire agreed in April has become a ceasefire in name only.

What the Traders Are Seeing

Tom Baker, Vitol's managing director for Bahrain — speaking at the S&P Global Energy Middle East conference in London — offered a warning that the oil market has been reluctant to hear: prices may still be too low.

Vitol is the world's largest independent oil trader, handling roughly 8 million barrels per day. Baker pointed out that 14 million barrels of Middle East supply are effectively offline — the largest supply disruption in history. China alone has lost 5 million barrels per day of imports.

"The turning point could be when someone really needs those physical molecules and the physical molecules just aren't there to buy," Baker said.

Goldman Sachs reinforced the message on Monday, forecasting that refined fuel margins will remain 2 to 3 times higher than pre-war averages through the end of 2026. Diesel margins alone are expected to exceed pre-war forecasts by $19-26 per barrel. Global refinery utilisation rates are climbing toward all-time highs.

What It Means for India

India imports more than 80% of its crude oil. With the Hormuz strait effectively closed, it has been scrambling to diversify — buying from Venezuela (now its fourth-largest supplier at 427,000 barrels per day), deepening ties with West African producers, and signing the new CEPA with Oman to route Gulf supplies around the blockade.

But every dollar added to the price of Brent widens India's current account deficit by roughly $2 billion per year. At $97, the deficit is already at levels that put pressure on the rupee, crowd out other imports, and feed into domestic inflation through transport and fertiliser costs.

The RBI has limited room to intervene. Foreign exchange reserves, while still substantial, have been declining as the central bank sells dollars to defend the rupee. Goldman Sachs last week named India the most vulnerable major economy on earth to the Hormuz disruption, estimating a potential GDP hit of 3.6%.

For Indian consumers, the arithmetic is simpler. Petrol and diesel prices, which the government has kept stable through election cycles by absorbing losses at oil marketing companies, are now at a level where further absorption may not be fiscally sustainable. A sustained period above $95-100 Brent typically forces a retail price revision.

Iran's missiles failed on Wednesday. The economic war they represent did not.
author: Diaspora Desk
